=========================

THE ORDER OF WORK
-----------------
1. Run USearch on a FASTA or target-decoy (.T-R) database. That writes a Family
   Cluster File (.fcf) next to the database: proteins grouped into families.
2. File -> Load Family Cluster File opens that .fcf. You are now in Layer 1 and
   can merge families further by description words or by keyword.
3. Layer 2: load the PatternLab project (.plp) that holds the quantitation. It
   must have been exported at PEPTIDE level - a protein-level export has nothing
   this program can attribute to a family.
4. Layer 3: choose what the percentage is OF, choose what to do with shared
   peptides, then press Recalculate.
5. Export to CSV, and/or File -> Reanotate Sepro to stamp the family numbers back
   into a SEPro result package.

The families and the quantitation you keep live in one FamilyQuant project file, a
.fqproj, written by File -> Save project. Beyond the share above, File -> Compute /
update full XIC measures each peptide's full isotope envelope straight from the RAW
and stores it in that project, and the Analytics screen then reads the recovery
from it. An old Family Cluster File (.fcf) still opens, with the quantitation empty
until it is computed.

WHAT THE PERCENTAGE IS OF (THE DENOMINATOR)
-------------------------------------------
A family's number is a share, and a share is meaningless until you know of what.
The list called "Report XIC as" is that choice. It currently reads:

    % of identified signal (families sum to 100%)

    Each family is divided by the sum of all families, so the column adds up
    to 100%. Always available, but the denominator moves with your database:
    identify more protein and every family's percentage changes. This is the
    default because it needs nothing recorded in the file.

No project is loaded, so the program cannot yet say which denominators this
data supports. Load one in Layer 2: the modes it cannot supply are greyed out,
each with the reason in its tooltip.

WHY THE FAMILIES DO NOT ADD UP TO 100%
--------------------------------------
In "% of identified signal" they do, by construction:
every family is divided by the sum of all families.

In "% of whole chromatogram" they do not, and that is
the point of the mode. The denominator is the whole chromatogram, and most of a
chromatogram is never identified: signal from peptides your database does not
contain, from non-peptide material, from charge states that were not extracted.
The gap between your families' total and 100% is that unidentified remainder. It is
a measurement, not an error - reading it as one is the mistake this mode exists to
prevent.

Under "Family-unique only (recommended)" a second piece is
missing as well: the signal on peptides that belong to more than one family and is
therefore counted for none of them.

WHAT A SHARED PEPTIDE IS
------------------------
A peptide whose sequence occurs in proteins of more than one family. In a venom
database, where whole families differ by a handful of residues, this is not a
corner case: most of the signal can sit on shared peptides. Nothing can say which
family such a peptide came from, so the program does not pretend to. In the Full
XIC column an identified peptide belongs to the families whose proteins contain
it, exactly as above; a de novo sequence, which has no protein of its own, to the
families of every protein it resembles at the minimum homology identity. The
choice is yours, and it is currently:

    Family-unique only (recommended)

    A peptide found in more than one family is counted for none of them. The
    families stay additive and can be read as a composition, at the cost of
    leaving out signal that cannot be assigned to a single family. This is
    the default and the right choice for anything you report.

    Split equally between families
        A shared peptide's signal is divided equally among the families it
        touches. The families still add up to the identified total, at the
        cost of assuming the signal is spread evenly between them.

    Count in every family (overlaps)
        A shared peptide is counted in full for every family it touches.
        This answers 'how much signal touches this family', but the families
        then OVERLAP: their percentages must not be added up, and on a
        redundant database they can total several times the whole sample.

--------------------------------------
Clustering runs in two stages. The fast first pass groups the database quickly,
but it is greedy and order-sensitive: two proteins that align above your identity
can still land in separate families, because the second was only ever compared
against the seed of a family it did not quite match. That leaves biological holes,
full-length homologues split apart.

The "Exhaustive clustering" checkbox (on by default) closes them. After the first
pass it aligns EVERY pair of proteins in full and merges two families whenever the
proteins reach your identity over most of the LONGER sequence. Proteins that share
only a short motif fail that coverage test and are correctly kept apart, so an
angiotensin fragment does not pull in a whole metalloproteinase, but two full-length
metalloproteinases the fast pass split are put back together.

This is single linkage: every pair at or above the identity chains its two families
into one, so the merge can chain a whole superfamily together. That is the intended
meaning of the threshold, not a side effect: the identity you choose IS the tightness
knob. Raise it for more, smaller families; lower it to chain more together.

The exhaustive pass runs at any database size and is never capped. On a database
over 10,000 sequences the all-versus-all alignment takes longer and more memory, so
you are warned once before it starts and can proceed or stop; it still runs at any
size if you proceed. Turn the checkbox off to use the faster first-pass-only
clustering, which is quicker but leaves the holes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
Undo steps back through the changes you make in Layer 1, one at a time, without
reloading the file. It reverses a Recluster by Words, a Create Super Cluster, a
User ID number you changed, or a lock you removed, putting the family numbers and
the locks back exactly as they were just before. It remembers the last 50 steps of
this session, does not survive closing the file, and there is no redo.

Create Super Cluster now offers two choices. "Match" decides whether one description
must contain ALL of your keywords or just ANY one of them; the default is "match all
words", so a phrase such as "acidic phospholipase" gathers only the acidic
phospholipases and leaves the plain ones alone, while "match any word" gathers
every family carrying even one keyword. A single keyword behaves the same either
way. The super cluster's own "Exclude Words" box keeps a protein OUT even when its
family matches: exclude "inhibitor" to gather the phospholipases without the
phospholipase inhibitor. It is separate from the Recluster by Words exclude box,
which drops words from the comparison rather than dropping a protein.
Separate its words with commas or spaces. It matches WHOLE words of the description
before OS=, and keeps out the proteins carrying the word; the rest of the family joins.

Create Super Cluster first shows a preview and changes nothing until you confirm.
Keywords find the families; every protein of those families is listed, each with a
tick, its Locus, its description as the database has it, and its domains. A protein
with none of your words is in red: it is here because another protein of its family
carries one, which is how a venom disintegrin comes along with a metalloproteinase.
Untick a protein and it stays in its family, while the rest of that family joins.
"Untick the red ones" does that for all of them at once. To untick many by hand,
click a heading to sort, Shift+click to select, and press Untick selected. When part
of a family leaves, the new family is locked, so that a Recluster by Words cannot put
back what you left out; the lock manager removes it. An annotation stays on each protein.

called "Disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein", so the word
ADAM finds nothing; the preview says so, and there they are on the list to untick.

type. If the Search box hides families that match, one tick brings them in.

in the file, with the UniProt release. They fill the Domains column, the Search box
finds them, and in the preview Keep domains unticks the proteins with none of the
domains you name: Reprolysin keeps those with the metalloproteinase domain whatever
they are called, and leaves out inhibitors and matrix metalloproteinases without a
single exclude word. A protein with no domains at all stays ticked if it carries a
keyword: the short disintegrins and many fragments are too short for Pfam. Domains do
not separate everything: most ADAMs have the same ones as a P-III SVMP.

description or to open its UniProt page. Ctrl+C copies the column you clicked, for
every selected row, or the whole row after a click on a row number.

"ribosomal protein" with "match any word" gathers either phrase. A phrase is
matched on the whole description, so a common word such as "protein", ignored as a
single keyword, still counts inside a phrase.

The Search box takes several terms separated by commas, for example
"metalloprotease, SVMP": a row is shown when it carries ANY of them.

Typing in the Search box now limits BOTH Recluster by Words and Create Super

numbers untouched, so you can organise one subgroup at a time. The word vectors are
then computed within the shown families, which is the intended "organise just this
subgroup" behaviour. The scope follows the SEARCH TEXT only, not the Hide Reverse
or Hide Contaminants checkboxes, so hiding rows for display never silently drops a
family from a recluster. Clear the Search box and both act on the whole database
again, exactly as before. Locks still hold within the subgroup.

WHY DIVIDE AND CONQUER GIVES A FLOOR, NOT A RECOMMENDATION
---------------------------------------------------------
Divide and Conquer searches for the lowest sequence identity at which no family
holds both a target and a decoy sequence. It is tempting to read its answer as
"the right identity". It is not, for a reason built into what the score can see.

A reversed database has the same internal redundancy as the real one: if two
proteins are similar, their reversed copies are similar too. So decoy families
collapse at the same rate as target families, and putting two decoys together is
not an error. The only event the score can detect is a target aligning to a decoy,

care about. The number it gives you is a floor, not a recommendation.

So: cluster at that identity or above, and

-----------------

                 renumbered a family by hand.
User ID          your own family number. Editable: change it and the families are

                 written back by Reanotate Sepro.
User Annotation  free text, saved in the .fcf and exported. It also NAMES the family

                 evidence pack. A family without one is named by the protein name
                 most of its members share (read before "OS=", "(Fragment)"
                 ignored); a tie goes to the first member in the table's order.
Locus            the protein identifier as it appears in the database.
Residue mass     the sum of the protein's amino-acid residue masses, in daltons.

they never change a number: hiding decoys or contaminants lowers the visible count
and leaves every percentage exactly as it was. In "% of identified signal" the hidden rows
are still inside the denominator, because that denominator is the sum over all
families, filtered or not.

Export to CSV writes exactly the rows you can see, with the values as fractions
between 0 and 1 and a dot as the decimal separator, whatever your machine's
language is. That is on purpose: the file is meant to be read by a program.

holds both a target and a decoy sequence. It is tempting to read its answer as
"the right identity". It is not, for a reason built into what the score can see.

A reversed database has the same internal redundancy as the real one: if two
proteins are similar, their reversed copies are similar too. So decoy families
collapse at the same rate as target families, and putting two decoys together is
not an error. The only event the score can detect is a target aligning to a decoy,
which happens once alignments have stopped being better than noise.

It therefore marks the identity below which clustering is meaningless. It CANNOT
see two unrelated target families being fused, which is the error you actually
care about. The number it gives you is a floor, not a recommendation.

So: cluster at that identity or above, and
choose the exact value from "Scan identity range" and from the biology of your
proteins. Raising the allowance above 0 does not buy accuracy, it buys merges made
inside the noise.

THE OTHER COLUMNS
-----------------
USearch ID       the last automatic grouping (USearch, then any reclustering the
                 program ran). Read-only. It equals User ID except where you
                 renumbered a family by hand.
User ID          your own family number. Editable: change it and the families are
                 regrouped, the User column recalculated, and it is the number
                 written back by Analysis > Reannotate SEPro.
User Annotation  free text, saved in the .fcf and exported. It also NAMES the family
                 in the Full XIC composition CSV, the Results chart and the
                 evidence pack. A family without one is named by the protein name
                 most of its members share (read before "OS=", "(Fragment)"
                 ignored); a tie follows the stored member order, not the grid sort.
Locus            a UniProt accession where available, otherwise the database identifier.
                 Hover over a cell for the full original identifier, kept in the file.
Residue mass     the sum of the protein's amino-acid residue masses, in daltons.
                 It does NOT include the terminal water: add 18.011 Da for the
                 neutral protein, and 1.007 Da more for the protonated (MH+) mass.
                 The column used to be called "Monoisotopic MH", which this number
                 has never been.

THE FAMILY COUNTER AND THE FILTERS
----------------------------------
The counter reads "N visible · M in file". Display and export filters hide rows,
they never change a number: hiding decoys or contaminants lowers the visible count
and leaves every percentage exactly as it was. In "% of identified signal" the hidden rows
are still inside the denominator, because that denominator is the sum over all
families, filtered or not.
Decoys are hidden by default; Show automatic IDs reveals the retained USearch ID.
Hide contaminants matches the case-sensitive prefix 'contaminant_', after one optional 'Reverse_' prefix.
It includes labelled keratins, trypsin and serum proteins; hiding them affects the
table and visible-row CSV only, so visible identified-signal shares can total below 100%.

Export to CSV writes exactly the rows you can see, with the values as fractions
between 0 and 1 and a dot as the decimal separator, whatever your machine's
language is. That is on purpose: the file is meant to be read by a program.

FILES, NAVIGATION AND KEYBOARD
Start actions also have menu commands; the status bar names the current stage and open project and explains what to do next. Tab and Shift+Tab move between enabled controls, and the native focus indicator marks the active control.

If no project is open, nothing is saved: use File > Open for a .fqproj or .fcf, or File > New from database to build families. File and row counts use whole numbers with digit grouping and no decimal places.

File > Save keeps families, User IDs, annotations and computed quantitation together in one .fqproj; use Save as to keep the previous version. The .fcf export keeps the families and annotations without the full XIC result.

Results reads stored full-envelope quantitation, including family shares and total-ion-current recovery, without reading RAW or changing families. Compute full XIC first when the project has no stored quantitation, then save the project to keep it.

The spectrum comparison is read-only, with one row per file, scan, charge and precursor m/z hypothesis, comparing PEAKS, DeepNovo and PatternLab. Its CSV export names the written CSV path in the completion message.


CURATION AND FAMILY SHARES
The recorded identity is the threshold used to build the file; higher identity gives more, smaller families, and changing it requires a new Build run. Align selected opens an alignment in a new window to check whether the selected family members are homologous.

Fetch evidence needs internet when the requested facts are not already cached; retrieved Pfam domains fill Domains, can be found by Search and can be selected in the grouping preview. Saving keeps them in the file, and family numbers stay unchanged by fetching.

Recluster by words merges descriptions meeting the similarity threshold, from 0.10 to 1.00; default 0.95 keeps near-identical wording, and lower it towards 0.90 to gather related descriptions. Family numbers change and percentages are recalculated; Undo restores the previous curation.

Ignore words accepts commas or spaces and is useful when a common word pulls unrelated families together. Ctrl+A selects all rows in the filtered protein view; Ctrl or Shift selects individual rows or ranges for User ID and annotation edits.

PatternLab projects must be exported at PEPTIDE level; a protein-level export makes every row read 0. The optional PatternLab share column stays empty until a project is loaded in PatternLab (optional), and Recalculate is unavailable until then.

For Full XIC, quantified signal gives family composition and total ion current gives each family's share of the whole sample, using the summed TIC of every recorded run. A Full XIC basis change applies at once.

The Full XIC summary accounts for families, peptides shared between families and peptides with no family. Export family composition writes CSV with one row per family and an unattributed row; its shared-peptide row appears only with Family-unique only.

Show quantified families only starts off and hides unquantified families without changing percentages. Hide decoys hides identifiers starting with Reverse_ from the table and CSV, without deleting data or changing percentages; show them while judging the clustering.

Manage locks is unavailable while no family is locked; removing a lock changes the open file immediately, and saving keeps it on disk. Apply grouping gathers the ticked proteins into one family and can be reversed with Undo; it is unavailable when there is no change to apply.



FAMILY PANEL AND EVIDENCE

File > Import family panel opens a draft for the open project. Choose a
spreadsheet, sheet and header row, then select the family key, name and
decision columns and, optionally, a Pfam column. Map every source decision
to Quantify, Report under others, Not a family or Merge into family. A merge
names the target family key. Preview the panel before applying it. Source
column text and the chosen mappings stay with the panel.

Keys must be unique within their scope. Add, edit or remove family rows in
the table. Multiple Pfam and subclass keys are separated by semicolons.
Unchanged keys keep their existing domain and subclass details.
Save panel as spreadsheet writes a reusable template. Its Families and
Subclasses sheets can be edited and imported again; the template also
retains panel details not shown in those sheets. The Subclasses sheet can
hold required and absent Pfam codes, source subfamily text and a report-as
key. Apply panel commits one project change; Undo can restore the prior
panel. Later assignment or subclass refresh operations have their own
Undo steps. Save the project to retain the change.

Check Pfam compares the panel's accessions and supplied names with the
provider. A mismatch, missing entry or unavailable check is shown; it
never silently changes the panel. A missing domain call is not proof that
a domain is absent.

Evidence grouping proposes family assignments from stored source evidence
and reviewed neighbours. Review and confirm ambiguous links between source
contexts and panel families, including an explicit outside-panel choice.
Apply only the proposals you accept. Unassigned or conflicting cases stay
visible rather than being guessed. Changing relevant panel rules can make
assignments and subclass labels out of date; rebuild them before use.

Subclass rules use the panel's required and absent domains or source
subfamily text. A fragment or missing evidence may not establish an
absence. Tied or incompatible evidence stays unresolved. A protein label
alone does not make a peptide unique to that subclass: shared peptide
evidence remains at the family or unresolved level when it cannot
distinguish a subclass.

FAMILY NUMBERS AND FIGURES

The composition headline is the mean of available per-run shares of the
signal credited to database families. The measured peptide signal and RAW
total ion current (TIC) are separate denominators; a peptide-signal share
is not a TIC share. Family-world-only signal is shown separately and is
not added to the database-family composition. These are signal shares,
not direct measurements of sample mass.

Run-to-run spread is the sample standard deviation, available only with
at least two runs. CV is that standard deviation divided by the mean and
is unavailable when the mean is zero. A run with a zero denominator has
an unavailable share, not zero. A pooled share sums signal across runs
before dividing and can differ from the mean of available per-run shares.
Where a measured-signal or TIC summary requires every run, missing values
leave that summary unavailable.

The protein count is a greedy estimate of the database proteins needed
to explain the observed peptides, not an exact minimum and not a gene
or proteoform count. A protein with a peptide of its own has an exactly
contained peptide unique among database targets, including labelled
contaminants; decoys are not targets. Shared evidence can support the
greedy explanation; homology-only matches can remain
unexplained. Read the unexplained count beside the estimate. Abundance
and the number of explanatory proteins answer different questions.

A family goes to Others when its mean share is strictly below the report
threshold, or when its panel decision is Report under others. The default
threshold is 0.1 percent and can be changed in Export report. The
member list retains the individual families and the reason for grouping.
Excluded panel rows are not families. A numeric family that conflicts
between panel keys or mixes panel and outside members stays a separate
flagged row rather than being assigned or added to Others.

Sensitivity comparisons, when stored, show how results change with the
selected shared-peptide policy and de novo cutoff. A missing combination
is unavailable, not an invented result. Count in every family overlaps:
those contributions cannot be summed as a normalized composition.

Family bars show mean shares with sample-SD whiskers when available.
Subclass stacks and the family/subclass ring use their stated pooled
basis; read their captions rather than equating pooled values with run
means. When available, the ring uses the same Others membership as the
report. The
abundance-versus-diversity plot pairs share with the greedy protein
estimate. A coverage map shows the stored protein positions, domains and
supported peptide placements; missing or ambiguous positions stay
unavailable or unresolved. The signal-source figure separates identified,
database-matched de novo and family-world-only contributions. Other
quality figures retain their own denominators and captions.

REPORT AND SUPPLEMENT

File > Report details stores the title, authors, sample description,
workflow, database kind and your written interpretation in the project.
Recorded input provenance is shown there. The interpretation is your own
text; check that any numbers it quotes are present in the report.

File > Export report needs stored Results. Choose sections and figures;
clearing a section removes its contents, and clearing a figure removes
that figure. The choices and report threshold can be saved in the project.
The report uses the project's own facts and the Light export palette.
Missing studies are identified as unavailable rather than filled in.
When a companion supplement is produced, use it for the long tables and
the individual families grouped as Others. Exporting a report does not
save the project: use File > Save to retain the choices and details for
a later export.

-----------------
1. Run USearch on a FASTA or target-decoy (.T-R) database. That writes a Family
   Cluster File (.fcf) next to the database: proteins grouped into families.
2. File -> Load Family Cluster File opens that .fcf. You are now in Layer 1 and
   can merge families further by description words or by keyword.
3. Layer 2: load the PatternLab project (.plp) that holds the quantitation. It
   must have been exported at PEPTIDE level - a protein-level export has nothing
   this program can attribute to a family.
4. Layer 3: choose what the percentage is OF, choose what to do with shared
   peptides, then press Recalculate.
5. Export to CSV, and/or File -> Reanotate Sepro to stamp the family numbers back
   into a SEPro result package.

The families and the quantitation you keep live in one FamilyQuant project file, a
.fqproj, written by File -> Save project. Beyond the share above, File -> Compute /
update full XIC measures each peptide's full isotope envelope straight from the RAW
and stores it in that project, and the Analytics screen then reads the recovery
from it. An old Family Cluster File (.fcf) still opens, with the quantitation empty
until it is computed.

WHAT THE PERCENTAGE IS OF (THE DENOMINATOR)
-------------------------------------------
A family's number is a share, and a share is meaningless until you know of what.
The list called "Report XIC as" is that choice. It currently reads:

    % of identified signal (families sum to 100%)

    Each family is divided by the sum of all families, so the column adds up
    to 100%. Always available, but the denominator moves with your database:
    identify more protein and every family's percentage changes. This is the
    default because it needs nothing recorded in the file.

No project is loaded, so the program cannot yet say which denominators this
data supports. Load one in Layer 2: the modes it cannot supply are greyed out,
each with the reason in its tooltip.

WHY THE FAMILIES DO NOT ADD UP TO 100%
--------------------------------------
In "% of identified signal" they do, by construction:
every family is divided by the sum of all families.

In "% of whole chromatogram" they do not, and that is
the point of the mode. The denominator is the whole chromatogram, and most of a
chromatogram is never identified: signal from peptides your database does not
contain, from non-peptide material, from charge states that were not extracted.
The gap between your families' total and 100% is that unidentified remainder. It is
a measurement, not an error - reading it as one is the mistake this mode exists to
prevent.

Under "Family-unique only (recommended)" a second piece is
missing as well: the signal on peptides that belong to more than one family and is
therefore counted for none of them.

WHAT A SHARED PEPTIDE IS
------------------------
A peptide whose sequence occurs in proteins of more than one family. In a venom
database, where whole families differ by a handful of residues, this is not a
corner case: most of the signal can sit on shared peptides. Nothing can say which
family such a peptide came from, so the program does not pretend to. In the Full
XIC column an identified peptide belongs to the families whose proteins contain
it, exactly as above; a de novo sequence, which has no protein of its own, to the
families of every protein it resembles at the minimum homology identity. The
choice is yours, and it is currently:

    Family-unique only (recommended)

    A peptide found in more than one family is counted for none of them. The
    families stay additive and can be read as a composition, at the cost of
    leaving out signal that cannot be assigned to a single family. This is
    the default and the right choice for anything you report.

The other options:

    Split equally between families
        A shared peptide's signal is divided equally among the families it
        touches. The families still add up to the identified total, at the
        cost of assuming the signal is spread evenly between them.

    Count in every family (overlaps)
        A shared peptide is counted in full for every family it touches.
        This answers 'how much signal touches this family', but the families
        then OVERLAP: their percentages must not be added up, and on a
        redundant database they can total several times the whole sample.

HOW THE FAMILIES ARE BUILT: TWO STAGES
--------------------------------------
Clustering runs in two stages. The fast first pass groups the database quickly,
but it is greedy and order-sensitive: two proteins that align above your identity
can still land in separate families, because the second was only ever compared
against the seed of a family it did not quite match. That leaves biological holes,
full-length homologues split apart.

The "Exhaustive clustering" checkbox (on by default) closes them. After the first
pass it aligns EVERY pair of proteins in full and merges two families whenever the
proteins reach your identity over most of the LONGER sequence. Proteins that share
only a short motif fail that coverage test and are correctly kept apart, so an
angiotensin fragment does not pull in a whole metalloproteinase, but two full-length
metalloproteinases the fast pass split are put back together.

This is single linkage: every pair at or above the identity chains its two families
into one, so the merge can chain a whole superfamily together. That is the intended
meaning of the threshold, not a side effect: the identity you choose IS the tightness
knob. Raise it for more, smaller families; lower it to chain more together.

The exhaustive pass runs at any database size and is never capped. On a database
over 10,000 sequences the all-versus-all alignment takes longer and more memory, so
you are warned once before it starts and can proceed or stop; it still runs at any
size if you proceed. Turn the checkbox off to use the faster first-pass-only
clustering, which is quicker but leaves the holes.

CURATING BY HAND: UNDO, SUPER CLUSTER OPTIONS, SEARCH-SCOPED RECLUSTERING
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Undo steps back through the changes you make in Layer 1, one at a time, without
reloading the file. It reverses a Recluster by Words, a Create Super Cluster, a
User ID number you changed, or a lock you removed, putting the family numbers and
the locks back exactly as they were just before. It remembers the last 50 steps of
this session, does not survive closing the file, and there is no redo.

Create Super Cluster now offers two choices. "Match" decides whether one description
must contain ALL of your keywords or just ANY one of them; the default is "match all
words", so a phrase such as "acidic phospholipase" gathers only the acidic
phospholipases and leaves the plain ones alone, while "match any word" gathers
every family carrying even one keyword. A single keyword behaves the same either
way. The super cluster's own "Exclude Words" box keeps a protein OUT even when its
family matches: exclude "inhibitor" to gather the phospholipases without the

which drops words from the comparison rather than dropping a protein.

tick, its Locus, its description as the database has it, and its domains. A protein
with none of your words is in red: it is here because another protein of its family

called "Disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein", so the word

type. If the Search box hides families that match, one tick brings them in.

single keyword, still counts inside a phrase.

The Search box takes several terms separated by commas, for example

So: cluster at that identity or above, and

                 most of its members share (read before "OS=", "(Fragment)"
                 ignored); a tie goes to the first member in the table's order.

The optional PatternLab .plp supplies the 'Share of signal' column.
Shared peptides applies to both columns; PatternLab share of and Recalculate apply
to the .plp column. Share of under Full XIC changes that column immediately.
Each share column names its denominator; Full XIC details and PatternLab details
retain the source facts. The bottom status line describes the PatternLab calculation.

THE ORDER OF WORK
-----------------
1. File > New from database opens Build. Choose database, then Build families on
   a FASTA or target-decoy (.T-R) database. That writes a Family
   Cluster File (.fcf) next to the database: proteins grouped into families.
2. File > Open opens that .fcf in Families, where you
   can merge families further by description words or by keyword.
3. Analysis > Compute full XIC opens Quantify for the primary quantitation route.
   In Families, PatternLab (optional) offers Load PatternLab project for a .plp. It
   must have been exported at PEPTIDE level - a protein-level export has nothing
   this program can attribute to a family.
4. In Quantitation, choose Shared peptides for either source. Share of applies to
   Full XIC immediately; PatternLab share of needs Recalculate for the .plp column.
5. File > Export writes CSV; Analysis > Reannotate SEPro stamps the family numbers back
   into a SEPro result package.

The families and the quantitation you keep live in one FamilyQuant project file, a
.fqproj, written by File > Save. Beyond the share above, Analysis > Compute full XIC
opens Quantify, which measures each peptide's full isotope envelope straight from the RAW
and stores it in that project, and the Results screen then reads the recovery
from it. An old Family Cluster File (.fcf) still opens, with the quantitation empty
until it is computed.

WHAT THE PERCENTAGE IS OF (THE DENOMINATOR)
-------------------------------------------
A family's number is a share, and a share is meaningless until you know of what.
For the optional .plp column, PatternLab share of is that choice. It currently reads:

    % of identified signal (families sum to 100%)

    Each family is divided by the sum of all families, so the column adds up
    to 100%. Always available, but the denominator moves with your database:
    identify more protein and every family's percentage changes. This is the
    default because it needs nothing recorded in the file.

No PatternLab project is loaded, so the program cannot yet say which .plp denominators
are available. Use Load PatternLab project: unsupported modes are greyed out,
each with the reason in its tooltip.

WHY THE FAMILIES DO NOT ADD UP TO 100%
--------------------------------------
In "% of identified signal" they do, by construction:
every family is divided by the sum of all families.

In "% of whole chromatogram" they do not, and that is
the point of the mode. The denominator is the whole chromatogram, and most of a
chromatogram is never identified: signal from peptides your database does not
contain, from non-peptide material, from charge states that were not extracted.
The gap between your families' total and 100% is that unidentified remainder. It is
a measurement, not an error - reading it as one is the mistake this mode exists to
prevent.

Under "Family-unique only (recommended)" a second piece is
missing as well: the signal on peptides that belong to more than one family and is
therefore counted for none of them.

WHAT A SHARED PEPTIDE IS
------------------------
A peptide whose sequence occurs in proteins of more than one family. In a redundant
database, where whole families differ by a handful of residues, this is not a
corner case: most of the signal can sit on shared peptides. Nothing can say which
family such a peptide came from, so the program does not pretend to. In the Full
XIC column an identified peptide belongs to the families whose proteins contain
it, exactly as above; a de novo sequence, which has no protein of its own, to the
families of every protein it resembles at the minimum homology identity. The
choice is yours, and it is currently:

    Family-unique only (recommended)

    A peptide found in more than one family is counted for none of them. The
    families stay additive and can be read as a composition, at the cost of
    leaving out signal that cannot be assigned to a single family. This is
    the default and the right choice for anything you report.

The other options:

    Split equally between families
        A shared peptide's signal is divided equally among the families it
        touches. The families still add up to the identified total, at the
        cost of assuming the signal is spread evenly between them.

    Count in every family (overlaps)
        A shared peptide is counted in full for every family it touches.
        This answers 'how much signal touches this family', but the families
        then OVERLAP: their percentages must not be added up, and on a
        redundant database they can total several times the whole sample.

HOW THE FAMILIES ARE BUILT: TWO STAGES
--------------------------------------
Clustering runs in two stages. The fast first pass groups the database quickly,
but it is greedy and order-sensitive: two proteins that align above your identity
can still land in separate families, because the second was only ever compared
against the seed of a family it did not quite match. That leaves biological holes,
full-length homologues split apart.

The "Exhaustive second pass" checkbox (on by default) closes them. After the first
pass it aligns EVERY pair of proteins in full and merges two families whenever the
proteins reach your identity over most of the LONGER sequence. Proteins that share
only a short motif fail that coverage test and are correctly kept apart, so an
angiotensin fragment does not pull in a whole metalloproteinase, but two full-length
metalloproteinases the fast pass split are put back together.

This is single linkage: every pair at or above the identity chains its two families
into one, so the merge can chain a whole superfamily together. That is the intended
meaning of the threshold, not a side effect: the identity you choose IS the tightness
knob. Raise it for more, smaller families; lower it to chain more together.

The exhaustive pass runs at any database size and is never capped. On a database
over 10,000 sequences the all-versus-all alignment takes longer and more memory, so
you are warned once before it starts and can proceed or stop; it still runs at any
size if you proceed. Turn the checkbox off to use the faster first-pass-only
clustering, which is quicker but leaves the holes.

THE FAMILY OVERVIEW AND PROTEIN TABLE
-------------------------------------
Families keeps the family overview, protein table and actions beside one another.
Select a family to show its proteins; All proteins restores the filtered protein
list. Each overview row shows its whole-family target count and one family share,
including members hidden by display filters; it never adds the repeated protein
shares together. Column headings name the current denominator.

Edit the family name to annotate every target member, including hidden members.
The family checkbox protects it from automatic grouping or removes that protection.
Each committed name or checkbox edit is one Undo step. Edit selected proteins can
join or split selected rows and set their annotation in one batch; destination and
surviving source families are locked, while emptied source families are not.

A legacy PatternLab export can lack the recorded divisor and per-run totals.
Re-exporting it from XQuant records the divisor and every run's totals, making
TIC reporting available when those totals are present; the other reporting modes
remain usable while that mode is greyed out.

CURATING BY HAND: UNDO, KEYWORD REVIEW, SEARCH-SCOPED RECLUSTERING
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Undo steps back through the changes you make in Families, one at a time, without
reloading the file. It reverses Recluster by words, Group by keywords, evidence
grouping, a family name or checkbox edit, a batch edit, a User ID edit or lock removal,
putting the changed family numbers, annotations and
the locks back exactly as they were just before. It remembers the last 50 steps of
this session, does not survive closing the file, and there is no redo.

Group by keywords opens Review grouping. "Match" decides whether one description
must contain ALL of your keywords or just ANY one of them; the default is "match all
words", so a phrase such as "acidic phospholipase" gathers only the acidic
phospholipases and leaves the plain ones alone, while "match any word" gathers
every family carrying even one keyword. A single keyword behaves the same either
way. The review's own "Exclude words" box keeps a protein OUT even when its
family matches: exclude "inhibitor" to leave out inhibitor descriptions while
the rest of a matching family joins. It is separate from the Recluster by words Ignore words box,
which drops words from the comparison rather than dropping a protein.
Separate its words with commas or spaces. It matches WHOLE words of the description
before OS=, and keeps out the proteins carrying the word; the rest of the family joins.

Group by keywords changes nothing until you confirm Apply grouping in the review.
Keywords find the families; every protein of those families is listed, each with a
tick, its Locus, its description as the database has it, and its domains. A protein
with none of your words is in red: it is here because another protein of its family
carries one, so a protein without a keyword can come along with a matching protein.
Untick a protein and it stays in its family, while the rest of that family joins.
"Untick the red ones" does that for all of them at once. To untick many by hand,
click a heading to sort, Shift+click to select, and press Untick selected. When part
of a family leaves, the new family is locked, so that Recluster by words cannot put
back what you left out; the lock manager removes it. An annotation stays on each protein.

A familiar protein name may be absent from the database description, so that keyword
can find nothing even for a protein you expected to include. The preview shows
the supplied descriptions and domains so you can decide which proteins to untick.
The keywords and exclude words can be edited there and everything follows as you
type. If the Search box hides families that match, one tick brings them in.

Fetch evidence asks UniProt for protein evidence, including Pfam domains, family,
keyword and tissue annotations, plus reviewed references for the families found.
The operation publishes the completed evidence and panel together; saving keeps them
in the file with their release for offline review. Pfam domains fill the Domains column; the Search box
finds them, and in the preview Keep domains unticks the proteins with none of the
domains you name: choosing a domain keeps proteins carrying it regardless of their
descriptions, and unticks noncarriers without an exclude word. A protein with no
domains stays ticked if it carries a keyword; short proteins and fragments can have
no Pfam call. Domains do not separate everything: different families can share them.

Fetch family world uses the confirmed database task and scope from Group by evidence.
Fetch evidence first to supply the database's family annotations.
If no matching task is confirmed, it reads the database and asks you to confirm the scope first.
The screen shows the stored release, scope, protein count and size. Cancel or a failed fetch
keeps the previous file. Save the project to keep the world for offline use. Compute uses the
stored world to populate Database gap, where credited tags can suggest FASTA additions.

Group by evidence opens the Evidence tab of Review grouping. Confirm the scope,
then review the supplied families, reasons, flags and protein ticks before Apply
grouping; the review's Help explains its architecture, motif and left-out views.
Cancelling leaves the open grouping unchanged and adds no Undo step.

In Review grouping and the Families protein table, right-click to copy a UniProt code or
description or to open its UniProt page. Ctrl+C copies the column you clicked, for
every selected row, or the whole row after a click on a row number.

Put words in quotes to require them together, in that order: "ribosomal subunit",
"ribosomal protein" with "match any word" gathers either phrase. A phrase is
matched on the whole description, so a common word such as "protein", ignored as a
single keyword, still counts inside a phrase.

The Search box takes several terms separated by commas, for example
"domain, fragment": a row is shown when it carries ANY of them.

Typing in the Search box limits both Recluster by words and Group by keywords
to the families the search shows: every family the search hides keeps its
numbers untouched, so you can organise one subgroup at a time. The word vectors are
then computed within the shown families, which is the intended "organise just this
subgroup" behaviour. The scope follows the SEARCH TEXT only, not the Hide decoys
or Hide contaminants checkboxes, so hiding rows for display never silently drops a
family from a recluster. Clear the Search box and both act on the whole database
again, exactly as before. Locks still hold within the subgroup.

WHY DIVIDE AND CONQUER GIVES A FLOOR, NOT A RECOMMENDATION
---------------------------------------------------------
Divide and Conquer searches for the lowest sequence identity at which no family
holds both a target and a decoy sequence. It is tempting to read its answer as
"the right identity". It is not, for a reason built into what the score can see.

A reversed database has the same internal redundancy as the real one: if two
proteins are similar, their reversed copies are similar too. So decoy families
collapse at the same rate as target families, and putting two decoys together is
not an error. The only event the score can detect is a target aligning to a decoy,
which happens once alignments have stopped being better than noise.

It therefore marks the identity below which clustering is meaningless. It CANNOT
see two unrelated target families being fused, which is the error you actually
care about. The number it gives you is a floor, not a recommendation.

So: cluster at that identity or above, and
choose the exact value from "Scan identity range" and from the biology of your
proteins. Raising the allowance above 0 does not buy accuracy, it buys merges made
inside the noise.

THE OTHER COLUMNS
-----------------
USearch ID       the last automatic grouping (USearch, then any reclustering the
                 program ran). Read-only. It equals User ID except where you
                 renumbered a family by hand.
User ID          your own family number. Editable: change it and the families are
                 regrouped, the User column recalculated, and it is the number
                 written back by Analysis > Reannotate SEPro.
User Annotation  free text, saved in the .fcf and exported. It also NAMES the family
                 in the Full XIC composition CSV, the Results chart and the
                 evidence pack. A family without one is named by the protein name
                 most of its members share (read before "OS=", "(Fragment)"
                 ignored); a tie follows the stored member order, not the grid sort.
Locus            a UniProt accession where available, otherwise the database identifier.
                 Hover over a cell for the full original identifier, kept in the file.
Residue mass     the sum of the protein's amino-acid residue masses, in daltons.
                 It does NOT include the terminal water: add 18.011 Da for the
                 neutral protein, and 1.007 Da more for the protonated (MH+) mass.
                 The column used to be called "Monoisotopic MH", which this number
                 has never been.

THE FAMILY COUNTER AND THE FILTERS
----------------------------------
The counter reads "N visible · M in file". Display and export filters hide rows,
they never change a number: hiding decoys or contaminants lowers the visible count
and leaves every percentage exactly as it was. In "% of identified signal" the hidden rows
are still inside the denominator, because that denominator is the sum over all
families, filtered or not.
Decoys are hidden by default; Show automatic IDs reveals the retained USearch ID.
Hide contaminants matches the case-sensitive prefix 'contaminant_', after one optional 'Reverse_' prefix.
It includes labelled keratins, trypsin and serum proteins; hiding them affects the
table and visible-row CSV only, so visible identified-signal shares can total below 100%.

Export to CSV writes exactly the rows you can see, with the values as fractions
between 0 and 1 and a dot as the decimal separator, whatever your machine's
language is. That is on purpose: the file is meant to be read by a program.

FILES, NAVIGATION AND KEYBOARD
Start actions also have menu commands; the status bar names the current stage and open project and explains what to do next. Tab and Shift+Tab move between enabled controls, and the native focus indicator marks the active control.

If no project is open, nothing is saved: use File > Open for a .fqproj or .fcf, or File > New from database to build families. File and row counts use whole numbers with digit grouping and no decimal places.

File > Save keeps families, User IDs, annotations and computed quantitation together in one .fqproj; use Save as to keep the previous version. The .fcf export keeps the families and annotations without the full XIC result.

Results reads stored full-envelope quantitation, including family shares and total-ion-current recovery, without reading RAW or changing families. Compute full XIC first when the project has no stored quantitation, then save the project to keep it.

The spectrum comparison is read-only, with one row per file, scan, charge and precursor m/z hypothesis, comparing PEAKS, DeepNovo and PatternLab. Its CSV export names the written CSV path in the completion message.


CURATION AND FAMILY SHARES
The recorded identity is the threshold used to build the file; higher identity gives more, smaller families, and changing it requires a new Build run. Align selected opens an alignment in a new window to check whether the selected family members are homologous.

Fetch evidence needs internet when the requested facts are not already cached; retrieved Pfam domains fill Domains, can be found by Search and can be selected in the grouping preview. Saving keeps them in the file, and family numbers stay unchanged by fetching.

Recluster by words merges descriptions meeting the similarity threshold, from 0.10 to 1.00; default 0.95 keeps near-identical wording, and lower it towards 0.90 to gather related descriptions. Family numbers change and percentages are recalculated; Undo restores the previous curation.

Ignore words accepts commas or spaces and is useful when a common word pulls unrelated families together. Ctrl+A selects all rows in the filtered protein view; Ctrl or Shift selects individual rows or ranges for User ID and annotation edits.

PatternLab projects must be exported at PEPTIDE level; a protein-level export makes every row read 0. The optional PatternLab share column stays empty until a project is loaded in PatternLab (optional), and Recalculate is unavailable until then.

For Full XIC, quantified signal gives family composition and total ion current gives each family's share of the whole sample, using the summed TIC of every recorded run. A Full XIC basis change applies at once.

The Full XIC summary accounts for families, peptides shared between families and peptides with no family. Export family composition writes CSV with one row per family and an unattributed row; its shared-peptide row appears only with Family-unique only.

Show quantified families only starts off and hides unquantified families without changing percentages. Hide decoys hides identifiers starting with Reverse_ from the table and CSV, without deleting data or changing percentages; show them while judging the clustering.

Manage locks is unavailable while no family is locked; removing a lock changes the open file immediately, and saving keeps it on disk. Apply grouping gathers the ticked proteins into one family and can be reversed with Undo; it is unavailable when there is no change to apply.



FAMILY PANEL AND EVIDENCE

File > Import family panel opens a draft for the open project. Choose a
spreadsheet, sheet and header row, then select the family key, name and
decision columns and, optionally, a Pfam column. Map every source decision
to Quantify, Report under others, Not a family or Merge into family. A merge
names the target family key. Preview the panel before applying it. Source
column text and the chosen mappings stay with the panel.

Keys must be unique within their scope. Add, edit or remove family rows in
the table. Multiple Pfam and subclass keys are separated by semicolons.
Unchanged keys keep their existing domain and subclass details.
Save panel as spreadsheet writes a reusable template. Its Families and
Subclasses sheets can be edited and imported again; the template also
retains panel details not shown in those sheets. The Subclasses sheet can
hold required and absent Pfam codes, source subfamily text and a report-as
key. Apply panel commits one project change; Undo can restore the prior
panel. Later assignment or subclass refresh operations have their own
Undo steps. Save the project to retain the change.

Check Pfam compares the panel's accessions and supplied names with the
provider. A mismatch, missing entry or unavailable check is shown; it
never silently changes the panel. A missing domain call is not proof that
a domain is absent.

Evidence grouping proposes family assignments from stored source evidence
and reviewed neighbours. Review and confirm ambiguous links between source
contexts and panel families, including an explicit outside-panel choice.
Apply only the proposals you accept. Unassigned or conflicting cases stay
visible rather than being guessed. Changing relevant panel rules can make
assignments and subclass labels out of date; rebuild them before use.

Subclass rules use the panel's required and absent domains or source
subfamily text. A fragment or missing evidence may not establish an
absence. Tied or incompatible evidence stays unresolved. A protein label
alone does not make a peptide unique to that subclass: shared peptide
evidence remains at the family or unresolved level when it cannot
distinguish a subclass.

FAMILY NUMBERS AND FIGURES

The composition headline is the mean of available per-run shares of the
signal credited to database families. The measured peptide signal and RAW
total ion current (TIC) are separate denominators; a peptide-signal share
is not a TIC share. Family-world-only signal is shown separately and is
not added to the database-family composition. These are signal shares,
not direct measurements of sample mass.

Run-to-run spread is the sample standard deviation, available only with
at least two runs. CV is that standard deviation divided by the mean and
is unavailable when the mean is zero. A run with a zero denominator has
an unavailable share, not zero. A pooled share sums signal across runs
before dividing and can differ from the mean of available per-run shares.
Where a measured-signal or TIC summary requires every run, missing values
leave that summary unavailable.

The protein count is a greedy estimate of the database proteins needed
to explain the observed peptides, not an exact minimum and not a gene
or proteoform count. A protein with a peptide of its own has an exactly
contained peptide unique among database targets, including labelled
contaminants; decoys are not targets. Shared evidence can support the
greedy explanation; homology-only matches can remain
unexplained. Read the unexplained count beside the estimate. Abundance
and the number of explanatory proteins answer different questions.

A family goes to Others when its mean share is strictly below the report
threshold, or when its panel decision is Report under others. The default
threshold is 0.1 percent and can be changed in Export report. The
member list retains the individual families and the reason for grouping.
Excluded panel rows are not families. A numeric family that conflicts
between panel keys or mixes panel and outside members stays a separate
flagged row rather than being assigned or added to Others.

Sensitivity comparisons, when stored, show how results change with the
selected shared-peptide policy and de novo cutoff. A missing combination
is unavailable, not an invented result. Count in every family overlaps:
those contributions cannot be summed as a normalized composition.

Family bars show mean shares with sample-SD whiskers when available.
Subclass stacks and the family/subclass ring use their stated pooled
basis; read their captions rather than equating pooled values with run
means. When available, the ring uses the same Others membership as the
report. The
abundance-versus-diversity plot pairs share with the greedy protein
estimate. A coverage map shows the stored protein positions, domains and
supported peptide placements; missing or ambiguous positions stay
unavailable or unresolved. The signal-source figure separates identified,
database-matched de novo and family-world-only contributions. Other
quality figures retain their own denominators and captions.

REPORT AND SUPPLEMENT

File > Report details stores the title, authors, sample description,
workflow, database kind and your written interpretation in the project.
Recorded input provenance is shown there. The interpretation is your own
text; check that any numbers it quotes are present in the report.

File > Export report needs stored Results. Choose sections and figures;
clearing a section removes its contents, and clearing a figure removes
that figure. The choices and report threshold can be saved in the project.
The report uses the project's own facts and the Light export palette.
Missing studies are identified as unavailable rather than filled in.
When a companion supplement is produced, use it for the long tables and
the individual families grouped as Others. Exporting a report does not
save the project: use File > Save to retain the choices and details for
a later export.
